section.title: The Covenant Confirmed
section.sectionRationale: This closes the giving of the law that began at Sinai: the people ratify the covenant in blood, seventy elders see God and eat before Him, and Moses ascends into the fire and cloud to receive the stone tablets and the pattern for the tabernacle.
section.thesis: Israel binds itself to the LORD with blood and a shared meal in His presence, and Moses then enters the consuming fire on the mountain to receive the tablets of the covenant.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the people ratify the covenant with blood and a covenant meal; the elders see the God of Israel and eat in His presence; Moses ascends into the cloud and fire of Sinai for forty days.

units.label: Blood of the covenant
units.note: all that the LORD has spoken we will do

media.alt: An altar with twelve pillars beneath a mountain
media.caption: Moses builds an altar and twelve pillars, then seals the covenant with blood.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Come up to the LORD, you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders, and you are to worship at a distance.
Moses alone shall approach the LORD, but the others must not come near. And the people may not go up with him.”
When Moses came and told the people all the words and ordinances of the LORD, they all responded with one voice: “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.”
And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. Early the next morning he got up and built an altar at the base of the mountain, along with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
Then he sent out some young men of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD.
Moses took half of the blood and put it in bowls, and the other half he sprinkled on the altar.
Then he took the {{covenant|Book of the Covenant}} and read it to the people, who replied, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.”
So Moses took the {{blood|blood}}, sprinkled it on the people, and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.”
Then Moses went up with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel,
and they saw the God of Israel. Under His feet was a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself.
But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.

units.label: Moses ascends the mountain
units.note: the glory of the LORD, a consuming fire

media.alt: A cloud covering a mountain summit
media.caption: Moses enters the cloud where the glory of the LORD burns like a consuming fire.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Come up to Me on the mountain and stay here, so that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.”
So Moses set out with Joshua his attendant and went up on the mountain of God.
And he said to the elders, “Wait here for us until we return to you. Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.”
When Moses went up on the mountain, the cloud covered it,
and the {{glory|glory}} of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai. For six days the cloud covered it, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud.
And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.
Moses entered the cloud as he went up on the mountain, and he remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

covenant.gloss: A covenant, a binding agreement sealed with obligations on both sides. The Book of the Covenant is the written record of what the LORD has just spoken, chapters 20 through 23, which the people now formally accept.

blood.gloss: Blood, the price of life offered in sacrifice. Sprinkled on both altar and people, it binds the two parties together and points to the life laid down that makes any covenant with a holy God possible.

glory.gloss: Glory, weightiness, the visible splendor of God's presence. Here it settles on Sinai as a consuming fire, showing that the God who now dwells among His people remains utterly holy and dangerous to approach carelessly.

basic.context: This chapter closes the giving of the law at Sinai. The people formally agree to the covenant, Moses seals it with blood, and then seventy elders go up the mountain and actually see God and share a meal in His presence. After that, Moses goes further up alone into the fire and cloud to receive the stone tablets and instructions for the tabernacle.
basic.hermeneutics: This really happened at a real mountain to a real, newly redeemed nation. It is the ratification ceremony for the old covenant, a specific historical event, though the pattern it sets, that God binds Himself to His people through blood and shares a meal with them, echoes forward into the New Testament.
basic.originalLanguages: The berith, covenant, is sealed with dam, blood, sprinkled on both the altar and the people, showing that both God and Israel are bound by this agreement through a costly sacrifice. Later, on the mountain, the kavod, glory, of the LORD appears as fire, showing His presence is both real and dangerous to those unprepared.
basic.typology: The blood of the covenant sprinkled on the people points forward to the blood of Christ, which Jesus Himself names at the Last Supper. The elders eating and drinking in God's presence anticipates the fuller fellowship believers now have with God and the future marriage supper of the Lamb.
basic.christ: At the Last Supper, Jesus takes the cup and says, 'This is My blood of the covenant,' deliberately echoing Moses' words here, Matthew 26:28. What Moses sealed with animal blood at Sinai, Christ seals forever with His own blood, establishing the new covenant that this old one anticipated.
basic.god: God is both near and terrifying: He allows elders to see Him and eat in His presence, yet His glory burns on the mountain like consuming fire, and only Moses may approach further. He binds Himself in covenant to His people while remaining utterly holy.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 26:27-28 records Jesus using the same covenant language over the cup. Hebrews 9:18-22 explains that the first covenant was not put into effect without blood. Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts the terror of Sinai with the access believers now have to God through Christ.
basic.oneStory: God seals His covenant with Israel in blood and lets its leaders eat in His presence, a real but partial fellowship. That pattern of covenant blood and a shared meal finds its fulfillment in Jesus, whose blood establishes the new covenant and whose table welcomes His people fully into God's presence.

context.literary:
Exodus 24 is built as a frame. Verses 1 and 2 give an instruction to come up the mountain, but the instruction is not carried out until verse 9. In between, verses 3 to 8 take place at the foot of Sinai, so the ceremony of blood is enclosed by the call to approach. The shape of the chapter makes a point before a word of commentary is offered: the way up the mountain runs through the altar.

The chapter also arranges people in rings of nearness. The whole nation stays at the base. Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and the seventy elders go part of the way and worship 'at a distance,' verse 1. Joshua goes further, verse 13. Moses alone enters the cloud, verse 18. Readers who go on into chapters 25 to 27 will meet the same pattern in cloth and wood: a courtyard for the people, a Holy Place for the priests, and a Most Holy Place for one man once a year.

The people's answer comes three times: in Exodus 19:8, in 24:3, and in 24:7, where it grows to 'we will do, and we will be obedient.' Between the second and third answers the words are written down, verse 4, and then read aloud, verse 7. The covenant moves from spoken word, to written word, to read word, to sealed word.

The closing verses echo creation. The cloud covers the mountain six days, and 'on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses,' verse 16. What follows, chapters 25 to 31, falls into seven speeches that each begin 'the LORD said to Moses,' and the seventh, Exodus 31:12-13, is about the Sabbath. The tabernacle is presented as a new creation in miniature.

Finally, the chapter sets a trap for chapter 32. There the people again offer burnt offerings and peace offerings, and 'sat down to eat and drink,' Exodus 32:6, the very words of 24:11, but now before a calf.
context.historical:
Covenants in the ancient Near East were made with recognisable steps, and first hearers would have known them. There was a written text, a public reading, witnesses, an oath, often a ritual involving slaughtered animals, and very often a shared meal. Jacob and Laban show the pattern on a small scale: a stone pillar as a witness, a sacrifice on the mountain, and a meal, Genesis 31:45-54. Exodus 24 contains every one of these elements, but the partners are not two chieftains. They are the LORD and a nation He has just redeemed from slavery, Exodus 20:2.

The twelve pillars of verse 4 are standing stones, a familiar way of marking a binding agreement. Joshua later sets up a stone under the oak at Shechem and says 'it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us,' Joshua 24:27. At Sinai each tribe has its stone, so no tribe could later claim it had not been party to the covenant.

The sacrifices are offered by 'young men of Israel,' verse 5, because the Aaronic priesthood had not yet been ordained; that comes in Exodus 28 and 29. Two kinds of offering are named. The burnt offering was wholly consumed on the altar. The peace offering was shared, with much of the meat eaten by the worshipers, Leviticus 7:15, which makes it likely that the meal of verse 11 drew on these sacrifices.

The people named are significant. Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's eldest sons, see God here and later die before Him for offering unauthorised fire, Leviticus 10:1-2. The seventy elders reappear when God shares Moses' Spirit with them, Numbers 11:16-17. Hur stood with Aaron holding up Moses' hands in battle, Exodus 17:12. The sapphire stone of verse 10 was probably the deep blue stone often called lapis lazuli, prized across the region and associated with the heavens. Moses' forty days, Deuteronomy 9:9 adds, were spent without bread or water.
context.canonical:
The phrase 'the blood of the covenant' travels through the rest of Scripture. Zechariah 9:11 grounds a promise of release on 'the blood of My covenant.' At the Last Supper Jesus takes up the words almost exactly, 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many,' Mark 14:24 and Matthew 26:28. Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 record it as 'the new covenant in My blood,' joining Exodus 24 to the promise of Jeremiah 31:31-34, a covenant 'not be like the covenant I made with their fathers.'

Hebrews quotes the verse directly, Hebrews 9:20, and draws out its logic: even the first covenant 'was not put into effect without blood,' Hebrews 9:18. It adds details from Israel's wider ritual practice, water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and it warns against treating 'the blood of the covenant' as common, Hebrews 10:29. Peter opens his first letter by describing believers as chosen 'for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood,' 1 Peter 1:2, the same order as Exodus 24:7-8, where the vow of obedience comes first and the sprinkling follows.

The vision of verses 10 and 11 has its own afterlife. Ezekiel sees 'the likeness of a throne with the appearance of sapphire,' Ezekiel 1:26. Isaiah foresees the LORD reigning on Zion 'before His elders with great glory,' Isaiah 24:23, and a banquet for all peoples on 'this mountain,' Isaiah 25:6. John sees twenty four elders around the throne, Revelation 4:4.

The ascent into the cloud also returns. Elijah goes forty days and nights to Horeb, 1 Kings 19:8. Jesus fasts forty days and nights, Matthew 4:2. On the mount of transfiguration, after six days, a cloud covers the disciples and a voice speaks from it, Matthew 17:1-5, with Moses himself present to see the glory now shining in the face of Jesus.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to understand that the covenant rests on grace and is sealed by God, not invented by them. The law they have just heard began with 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,' Exodus 20:2. Their pledge is an answer to rescue, not a bid for it.

He also wants them to feel the weight of their own words. Three times they have said 'we will do.' The words are recorded, read back to them, and then sealed with blood thrown over them. A later generation reading this chapter would know exactly what their ancestors promised, and would read chapter 32 with a sinking heart.

At the same time, the chapter shows the astonishing hospitality of God. Leaders of a nation of former slaves eat a meal in the presence of the God whose voice had made them beg for distance, Exodus 20:19. Moses wants Israel to know that the goal of the covenant is fellowship.

Finally, the chapter insists on mediation. Only Moses goes into the cloud, and the tablets and the pattern for the tabernacle come down through him. Israel is meant to see that access to God is real, graded and given, and that it comes through the one God appoints.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The ceremony itself is descriptive. It happened once, at one mountain, and no later passage tells Israel to repeat it. Christians are not asked to build pillars, sprinkle blood, or climb mountains to meet God. Hebrews explicitly contrasts the church's standing with Sinai: 'you have not come to a mountain that can be touched,' Hebrews 12:18.

Yet the chapter carries instruction by pattern. The Lord's Supper is commanded, 'do this in remembrance of Me,' 1 Corinthians 11:25, and it is the new covenant meal that Exodus 24 foreshadows, eaten by people who have been cleansed by blood and welcomed to God's table.

The people's vow teaches by example too, but carefully. Their words were right; God Himself said of a similar pledge, 'They have done well in all that they have spoken,' Deuteronomy 5:28, and then added, 'If only they had such a heart,' Deuteronomy 5:29. What chapter 32 exposes is that sincere promises cannot by themselves keep a covenant. The application is not to stop promising obedience, but to make those promises as people who lean on the blood and the Mediator rather than on the strength of their resolve.

debates.question: What does it mean that the elders 'saw the God of Israel' and yet lived, when Exodus 33:20 says no one can see God and live?

views.label: A veiled or partial theophany
views.case: They saw a visible manifestation of God's presence and not His unveiled being. The text itself is restrained: it describes only what was 'under His feet,' verse 10, as if the witnesses could not raise their eyes higher. Exodus 33:20-23 later distinguishes between God's face, which cannot be seen, and a lesser sight that can.

views.label: An appearance of the Son before the incarnation
views.case: Some read this as a Christophany. John 1:18 says 'No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son... has made Him known,' which suggests that Old Testament appearances of God were appearances of the Son, the one who reveals the Father.

views.label: A vision granted in a prophetic mode
views.case: Others note that verse 11 uses a verb that commonly describes prophetic seeing, so the elders were given a vision of God rather than bodily sight, much as Isaiah and Ezekiel later 'saw' the Lord enthroned, Isaiah 6:1 and Ezekiel 1:26-28.

debates.bearing: The views overlap more than they compete. All agree the encounter was real, gracious and limited, and that the text stresses God's restraint, 'God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel,' more than the details of what was seen.

debates.question: What does the sprinkling of blood on the altar and the people signify?

views.label: A binding oath under penalty
views.case: Ancient covenant rites often used slain animals to picture the fate of a partner who broke faith. Genesis 15:9-17 and Jeremiah 34:18-20 show animals cut in two, with covenant breakers treated 'like the calf they cut in two.' On this view the blood says: may our life be forfeit if we fail to keep these words.

views.label: Consecration to a holy God
views.case: The nearest parallel is the ordination of the priests, Exodus 29:20-21, where blood and oil 'consecrated' Aaron and his sons. On this view the nation is being set apart as 'a kingdom of priests,' Exodus 19:6, made fit to belong to God.

views.label: A bond of shared life
views.case: The blood is divided, half on the altar, which stands for God, and half on the people. One life is applied to both parties, joining them. Leviticus 17:11 teaches that 'the life of the flesh is in the blood,' so the covenant becomes a union of life, not only a contract.

debates.bearing: These readings are complementary. The blood seals an oath, consecrates a people and binds two parties together. The New Testament gathers all three when it speaks of blood that sanctifies, Hebrews 10:29, establishes a covenant, Mark 14:24, and gives life to those who share in it, John 6:54.

study.originalLanguages:
The people's final answer in verse 7 is na'aseh venishma, literally 'we will do and we will hear.' The second verb, shama, is the ordinary word for hearing, but it regularly carries the sense of heeding, which is why the BSB renders it 'we will be obedient.' The same verb stood at the head of the Sinai offer: 'if you will indeed obey My voice,' Exodus 19:5. Hebrew does not separate listening from obeying the way English does. To hear God rightly is already to respond.

In verse 8 the LORD 'has made' a covenant, and the verb is karat, 'to cut.' Hebrew speaks of cutting a covenant, an idiom that probably grows from the practice of cutting animals in covenant rites, Genesis 15:10 and Jeremiah 34:18. In Exodus 24 the cutting language and the blood belong together.

The verb for sprinkling in verses 6 and 8 is zaraq, which pictures a generous tossing or dashing of liquid rather than a few drops. It is the regular verb for blood thrown against the altar in the sacrificial laws, Leviticus 1:5. Here it is used for the people as well as the altar, so the whole nation is drenched in the same blood that marked the altar.

Verses 10 and 11 use two different verbs for seeing. Verse 10 has the common ra'ah, 'they saw.' Verse 11 has chazah, a verb that often belongs to prophetic vision and gives its name to the seer. The shift slows the reader down: this was a seeing of a special kind. The pavement under His feet is literally 'a work of the brick of sapphire.' The word for brick is related to the bricks of Egypt, Exodus 1:14 and 5:7. The people who laboured over mud bricks for Pharaoh now see their God standing on a pavement of heavenly blue.

The phrase 'did not lay His hand' in verse 11 is shalach yad, 'to stretch out the hand,' the expression God used for striking Egypt, Exodus 3:20. The hand that fell on Pharaoh is withheld from Israel's leaders.

In verse 16 the glory 'settled' on Sinai, from shakan, 'to dwell.' From the same root comes mishkan, the dwelling or tabernacle, which is exactly what God begins to describe in the next chapter, 'that I may dwell among them,' Exodus 25:8. The mountain is the first dwelling; the tent will carry it on the road.

Lastly, the 'consuming fire' of verse 17 is esh okhelet, literally 'eating fire.' The verb is akal, the same verb used in verse 11 when the elders 'ate.' The chapter sets the two side by side: the leaders eat in God's presence, and God's glory appears as fire that eats. What keeps the first from becoming the second is the blood of verse 8.

typology.type: The blood of the covenant, Exodus 24:8
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai the blood came from young bulls offered by young men, and it was thrown over the people to bind them to a covenant they would soon break. At the Last Supper Jesus takes Moses' very phrase and applies it to His own blood, 'poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28. The escalation lies in the source and the effect. The blood is His own, Hebrews 9:12, and it purifies the conscience, Hebrews 9:14, which animal blood could not do. The type falls short because it bound Israel to terms they could not keep; the new covenant writes the law on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33.

typology.type: The covenant meal on the mountain, Exodus 24:11
typology.fulfillment: Seventy elders ate and drank before God and were not struck down. The meal sealed the covenant and showed its purpose, fellowship with God. Jesus shares a covenant meal with the twelve and promises that they will 'eat and drink at My table in My kingdom,' Luke 22:30. The church's cup is 'a participation in the blood of Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:16, and the story ends at 'the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:9. The type falls short because it was for a few leaders at a distance; the gospel meal is for all God's people, and the final feast is for 'all the peoples,' Isaiah 25:6.

typology.type: Moses the mediator entering the cloud, Exodus 24:15-18
typology.fulfillment: Moses alone went into the glory and came back with the words of God and the pattern for His dwelling. Christ is 'the mediator of a new covenant,' Hebrews 9:15, and He entered not a mountain cloud but 'heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God,' Hebrews 9:24. Moses was faithful 'as a servant,' while Christ is faithful 'as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:5-6. The type breaks down at the point of access: Moses went in alone and the people stayed below, while Christ brings His people with Him into the Most Holy Place, Hebrews 10:19-20.

typology.type: The glory cloud on the mountain after six days, Exodus 24:16
typology.fulfillment: The cloud covered Sinai six days and God spoke from it on the seventh. The Gospels tell the transfiguration in the same colours: 'after six days' Jesus leads three disciples up a high mountain, His face shines, a bright cloud overshadows them and a voice from the cloud speaks, Matthew 17:1-5. Moses is present, and Luke says they spoke of Jesus' 'departure,' Luke 9:31. At Sinai the voice gave commandments; on the new mountain it points to a Person, 'Listen to Him!' The type falls short because Sinai's glory was seen from outside; in Jesus the glory shines in a human face, 2 Corinthians 4:6.

study.christ:
The strongest link between this chapter and Christ is made by Jesus Himself. On the night He was betrayed He took a cup and said, 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many,' Mark 14:24. No one in that room could miss the echo of Moses at the foot of Sinai. Jesus was saying that a new covenant was being inaugurated, and that its blood was His. Luke's account makes the link with Jeremiah explicit: 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20. The covenant Jeremiah promised would be 'not be like the covenant I made with their fathers,' Jeremiah 31:32, and the difference begins with the blood.

That difference runs deep. At Sinai the people pledged obedience and then the blood was applied. Under the new covenant the pledge rests on a better guarantee. Jesus 'has become the guarantee of a better covenant,' Hebrews 7:22, and God raised Him from the dead 'through the blood of the eternal covenant,' Hebrews 13:20. The weight of the covenant no longer hangs on the people's 'we will do,' but on what Christ has done.

The chapter also leads to Christ by the pattern of the meal. The elders ate and drank before God and He did not lay His hand on them. At the Last Supper the disciples ate and drank with God incarnate at the table, and He promised to drink the cup 'anew with you in My Father's kingdom,' Matthew 26:29. After the resurrection He was known to two disciples 'in the breaking of the bread,' Luke 24:30-35. The church's meal is a foretaste of the table the elders only glimpsed.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of mediation. Moses alone could go into the cloud. Paul insists there is 'one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,' 1 Timothy 2:5. Unlike Moses, who could only offer to be blotted out for the people's sin, Exodus 32:32, Christ actually bore it.

And it leads to Christ by the vision of glory. The elders saw only what was under God's feet. John says 'No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son... has made Him known,' John 1:18. Jesus prays that His people will 'see the glory You gave Me,' John 17:24.

A caution keeps this honest. The pillars, the bowls and the young men are not coded pictures of Christ. The links rest on the New Testament's own use of the chapter, especially the phrase 'blood of the covenant,' which Jesus chose deliberately.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who binds Himself. A covenant is not a mood or a passing favour; it is a committed relationship with stated terms. The LORD, who owes Israel nothing, puts His words in writing, verse 4, and lets them be read aloud to the whole nation, verse 7. God is willing to be held to His word. Half the blood goes on the altar, which represents Him, so that He is as much a party to the covenant as they are.

He is a God of ordered holiness. The instructions of verses 1 and 2 set boundaries before anything else happens: some come near, some worship at a distance, and one man goes all the way. That order is not stinginess. It is the shape that love takes when a holy God draws near to unholy people, and it protects them. Nadab and Abihu, who saw God here, later died for approaching in their own way, Leviticus 10:1-2. God's holiness does not change with familiarity.

He is also a God of astonishing welcome. The same nation that had begged not to hear His voice, Exodus 20:19, now sends its leaders up the mountain to eat before Him. The text slows down to say it twice: 'God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.' The purpose of His holiness is not to keep people away forever but to make it safe for them to come.

He is a God whose glory is both beautiful and dangerous. Beneath His feet the elders see something 'as clear as the sky itself,' verse 10. From the valley the people see 'a consuming fire,' verse 17. Scripture holds these together: 'the LORD your God is a consuming fire,' Deuteronomy 4:24, and Hebrews repeats it for Christians, Hebrews 12:29. The same glory that delights those who are covered frightens those who are not.

He is a God who speaks in His own time. For six days the cloud covers the mountain, and only on the seventh does He call, verse 16. Moses waits, and God is not hurried. The pause mirrors the rhythm of creation, Genesis 2:2, and teaches that access to God is on His terms.

For worship, the chapter calls for both joy and awe, which Hebrews joins in one sentence: 'let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe,' Hebrews 12:28. Believers come to God's table invited, cleansed by blood, and still aware that the One who welcomes them is fire.

crossReferences.note: The people's first answer, 'We will do everything that the LORD has spoken,' given before they had even heard the Ten Commandments. Exodus 24:3 and 24:7 repeat it, the last time with the added pledge of obedience. The threefold vow shows how sincere and how self-confident Israel was.

Jacob and Laban make a covenant with a stone pillar as witness, a heap of stones, a sacrifice on a mountain, and a shared meal. It shows the ordinary covenant customs that Exodus 24 takes up, now used for a covenant between God and a whole nation.

At the ordination of Aaron and his sons, blood from the altar is sprinkled on the priests and their garments, and they are consecrated. The echo suggests that the sprinkling at Sinai set the whole nation apart for God, in keeping with the calling to be 'a kingdom of priests,' Exodus 19:6.

Only weeks later the people offer burnt offerings and peace offerings again and 'sat down to eat and drink,' but before a golden calf. The deliberate echo of Exodus 24:5 and 24:11 shows the covenant meal turned into idolatry and the vow broken.

Nadab and Abihu, who saw God and ate before Him in Exodus 24:9-11, later offer unauthorised fire and are consumed. Having been near God does not make it safe to approach Him on one's own terms. The consuming fire of Exodus 24:17 is not a metaphor.

Jesus says, 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.' The wording follows Exodus 24:8 closely. At the table He declares that His own death inaugurates the covenant Moses' sacrifice only anticipated, and the cup becomes its sign.

God promises a new covenant, 'not be like the covenant I made with their fathers,' which they broke. The Sinai covenant sealed in Exodus 24 is the one in view. The new one will write the law on hearts and forgive sin, supplying what the vow at Sinai lacked.

Quotes Exodus 24:8 and argues that 'even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood.' Hebrews reads the ceremony as a lesson in how covenants with God are made, leading to the conclusion that 'without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.'

Peter describes believers as chosen 'for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood.' The order mirrors Exodus 24:7-8, where the pledge of obedience is followed by the sprinkling. The church is a covenant people constituted the way Israel was at Sinai, now by Christ's blood.

Contrasts Sinai, with its fire, darkness and terror, with Mount Zion, where believers come 'to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.' The sprinkled blood of Exodus 24 finds its better counterpart.

After six days Jesus leads three disciples up a high mountain, His face shines, a bright cloud overshadows them and a voice speaks from it. The scene deliberately recalls Exodus 24:16, but the voice now directs attention to the Son: 'Listen to Him!'

The LORD will prepare a banquet 'on this mountain' for all peoples and swallow up death forever. The meal of a few elders on Sinai becomes a feast for the nations, where the shroud over humanity is removed and God wipes away every tear.

study.oneStory:
In Eden humanity ate in God's presence freely, and lost that place by eating what He had forbidden. Ever since, the question of the Bible has been how sinful people can be with a holy God again. Exodus 24 gives the most vivid answer the Old Testament has yet offered. A redeemed people are bound to God by blood, and their leaders eat and drink before Him on His mountain and live.

The chapter looks back to the covenant with Abraham. God had cut a covenant with him among the divided animals, Genesis 15:9-18, and had promised to bring his descendants out of slavery. Sinai is that promise kept and extended. The nation now stands in covenant with the God of their fathers, marked by blood, holding His words in writing.

The chapter also looks forward, and not only to good things. The vow 'we will do' is broken at the golden calf, Exodus 32. The rest of Israel's history, from the judges to the exile, shows a people who meant their promises and could not keep them. The prophets respond not by abandoning the covenant but by promising a new one: blood that releases prisoners, Zechariah 9:11, and a law written on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33.

That new covenant arrives at a table in Jerusalem. Jesus takes the words of Moses and says the blood is His. His death does what the bulls at Sinai could not: it cleanses the conscience and secures the promised inheritance, Hebrews 9:14-15. His people now share a meal that is 'a participation in the blood of Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:16, and they come not to a burning mountain but to Mount Zion, Hebrews 12:22-24.

The story ends where this chapter points. The elders saw God's feet; in the new creation His servants 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The meal of seventy on a mountain becomes the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, a banquet for all peoples on the mountain of the LORD, where death is swallowed up forever, Isaiah 25:6-8. And the glory that settled on Sinai for a season settles among humanity for good: 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them,' Revelation 21:3.

quiz.q: How did the people respond when Moses told them all the words and ordinances of the LORD?

options.text: With one voice, they said, 'All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.'
options.note: Verse 3 records this unanimous response before Moses even writes the words down.

options.text: They asked for more time to consider the covenant terms.
options.note: No delay is recorded; their commitment was immediate and unanimous.

options.text: Only the elders agreed, while the rest of the people were silent.
options.note: The text says all the people responded with one voice, not only the elders.

options.text: They refused and asked Moses to renegotiate the terms.
options.note: The opposite occurred; they willingly agreed to obey all that the LORD had spoken.

quiz.q: How did Moses seal the covenant between the LORD and the people?

options.text: By sprinkling half the sacrificial blood on the altar and half on the people.
options.note: Verses 6 and 8 describe this two part sprinkling, calling it the blood of the covenant.

options.text: By having each tribal leader sign a written document.
options.note: Moses did write down the words, but the covenant was sealed with blood, not signatures.

options.text: By offering only incense on the altar.
options.note: Burnt offerings and peace offerings were made, and it was the blood, not incense, that sealed the covenant.

options.text: No sealing act took place.
options.note: Verses 6 through 8 explicitly describe the blood ceremony that sealed the covenant.

quiz.q: What happened when Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders went up the mountain?

options.text: They saw the God of Israel and ate and drank in His presence without harm.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11 record this remarkable, gracious encounter.

options.text: They were struck down for approaching too closely.
options.note: The text states plainly that God did not lay His hand on them; they were not harmed.

options.text: They saw nothing but heard only thunder.
options.note: The text specifically says they saw the God of Israel, more than mere thunder.

options.text: They were forbidden from ascending at all.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly says Moses went up with Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders.

quiz.q: How long did Moses remain on the mountain after entering the cloud?

options.text: Forty days and forty nights.
options.note: Verse 18 states this exact duration.

options.text: Seven days only.
options.note: The cloud covered the mountain for six days before the LORD called to Moses on the seventh, but Moses himself remained forty days and nights.

options.text: A single day.
options.note: The stay was far longer, forty days and nights.

options.text: The text does not specify a duration.
options.note: Verse 18 explicitly gives the forty day, forty night duration.

quiz.q: What did the glory of the LORD look like to the Israelites on the mountaintop?

options.text: Like a consuming fire.
options.note: Verse 17 describes it exactly this way, in the sight of all Israel.

options.text: Like a gentle mist with no visible color.
options.note: The text specifically describes fire, something far more overwhelming than a gentle mist.

options.text: Completely invisible to everyone but Moses.
options.note: The text says the Israelites themselves saw the sight of the glory of the LORD like consuming fire.

options.text: No visible sign accompanied God's presence.
options.note: Verse 17 explicitly describes the visible sight of consuming fire.

questions: The people said, 'All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do,' before they had faced any real test of that promise. Where in your own life have you made commitments to God more easily than you have kept them?
The covenant was sealed with blood, not merely words. How does remembering that your relationship with God cost the blood of Christ change the way you approach Him today?

The elders saw God and ate in His presence without being struck down, a real but bounded nearness. Where do you find yourself either presuming too much on God's nearness or fearing to draw near at all?
Moses left ordinary life behind for forty days to be with God on the mountain. What would it look like for you to give God unhurried, extended time this week rather than only brief, hurried moments?
God's glory appeared like consuming fire, both real and dangerous. How does holding together God's nearness and His holiness shape the way you pray and worship?

translationNotes.note: The Book of the Covenant most likely refers to the laws just given in chapters 20 through 23, which Moses had written down in verse 4; it is read aloud so the people know exactly what they are agreeing to.

Under His feet was a work like a pavement of sapphire describes what the elders saw beneath God, not His face or full form; the language is deliberately restrained, consistent with later statements that no one sees God's face and lives.

God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel is a Hebrew idiom meaning He did not strike them down, emphasizing that this vision of God, unlike other encounters with His holiness, brought no harm.
